utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case ... [Albanian on English Channel.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: ... [Albanian on English Channel]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a problem with the translation on channel 4. On channel 4, I would expect English. Yes, I think it's now fixed. First of all, there are two Judges. Judge Stole is not at this moment in The Hague. He was expected to come back early this morning, but due to medical conditions, Judge Stole is not available. The two remaining Judges have decided that it's in the interests of justice to continue hearing the case under Rule 15 bis. Then, perhaps, a brief explanation as far as the late start is concerned. More and more the Chamber needs the early morning minutes in order to digest the material that has come in at night. I'm, as a matter of fact, preparing a device on my computer, which wakes me up if something arrives in the middle of the night, so that we don't waste time in the morning. Courtesy copies, official filings, everything comes in; and, sometimes, we take and need time to further think about how to proceed. That certainly caused most of the delay of this morning. I do understand that the parties have suggestions as how to proceed today. I was informed that Mr. Emmerson would like to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: When the issue of the evidence that is proposed for today was raised yesterday afternoon, I indicated that there were two separate questions really running in parallel. The first is clarification of precisely which documentation the Prosecution proposes to adduce this evidence for; in other words, which additional documents, if any, over and above those that have already been admitted or tendered the chain of custody witnesses are intended to produce. The second is the mechanism for establishing chain of custody, given that we received last night a declaration dealing with handling and chain of custody within the OTP. There is this witness who deals with one stage of the documentation. There is a further witness who deals with another stage of the documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There's just a potential fracture between the two. Now, in the motion that was served last night at page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: By the way, has that been filed meanwhile? Because I -- part of the material to digest was a courtesy copy received yesterday at 7.00. Has that been filed?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It was a -- a courtesy copy of the electronic filing. When we filed it, we also sent a direct copy to the Trial Chamber and to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, but it has been -- I don't know exactly how this works, Mr. Registrar, if something is electronically filed, I don't know at what time it was filed, whether it's then on that date, and when is filing complete in that respect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The registry informed me that the filing is complete as soon as it's electronically received, although distribution may take place the next day if the material arrived after 4.00 p.m. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So, if Your Honours have pages 88 to 91 of the filing, which I'm not certain that the pagination necessarily corresponds electronically, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- there should be a schedule that looks like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's in front of me. That's part of our digestive work this morning. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Now, as we've understood the Prosecution position, the documents that would be tendered through the evidence of chain of custody witnesses fall into three categories: The first is documents that have already either been admitted or marked for identification, many of them through the testimony of Bislim Zyrapi, and that covers the list of documents on page 1 and 2. Then there is a category of three single sheets or very short documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- which are documents said by the Prosecution to be on the Rule 65 ter list but not yet tendered by the Prosecution. So they haven't been put through Zyrapi or any other witness, but Prosecution wishes to adduce those three documents. Then there is a third category of three documents that are not on the Rule 65 ter list, but where it is said that they have the same content as documents which are. I haven't had an opportunity overnight to ascertain whether the same content means that they are merely duplicative, in the sense that they are identical documents or whether it is that they are of broadly similar effect. Now, Your Honours will have seen from the material filed with the declaration that the pool of material, from which the collection of exhibits have been tendered or are sought to be tendered is drawn, is some 24 Lever Arch files of material, running to thousands of pages. Now, the clarity that I have been seeking for some time, as contingent upon whether or not these witnesses are required to give evidence, has been what exactly it is from amongst that material that is intended to form part of the Prosecution's case, and our understanding is it is these documents in this schedule and no more. If that is a correct understanding, which means that there are essentially six further documents over and above those that have already been either tendered or admitted, then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of which three apparently are for similar. Okay. Let's carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And three are on and three are off the existing 65 ter list, then that answers one part of the question and is extremely helpful and we all know where we stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Could we seek confirmation from Mr. Re that, as far as the chain of custody witnesses are concerned, that these are the documents which you seek from -- for which you seek to establish that the chain of custody was as the witnesses testify, or is there anything else, like what was in the suitcases that were traveling apparently, as we might hear from the witness, were coming from Kosovo to Novi Sad and to Belgrade? That's what I read in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in the statement, which, of course, still needs to be confirmed by the witness. Is it -- my question is clear, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your question is -- is very clear, and I agree the documents had a very interesting journey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but that was not the core of the problem. That was just my --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just looking in the decision of the - I'm sorry, it's just on the computer screen - of the 15th of October in relation to Mr. Zyrapi. There were two documents the Trial Chamber specifically asked us for information on the chain of custody. Those two documents we've referred to in the filing of yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are they on this list?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's P130 and P234.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And P234.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. They were on the list. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. They're in this list, and that's -- the purpose of this is to inform the Trial Chamber of the chain of custody --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But question was a different one. It is whether you limit yourself to these documents or whether through these witnesses you want to -- to seek an avenue to get anything more into evidence or to establish chain of custody on something which is not yet in evidence which is not on this list. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't know of anything else, apart from that list which we are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So, then, I may interpret the answer as being no, it's limited to these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think so. I'm 99 per cent sure that that's the purpose of it. I've --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I don't want to say 100 per cent, but I'm 99 per cent sure that that is the entirety of it. Mr. Emmerson earlier expressed concern about us trying to get 24 binders in, and that's simply not the case. It's to establish where the documents which are on the exhibit list came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand, but the 1 per cent certainly will make Mr. Emmerson, to the extent he's capable of becoming nervous, he would be nervous about 1 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I don't think "nervous" is the right word, but I would be concerned because that would involve the Defence and the Trial Chamber in taking time out now to go through each and every document and establish whether or not that material was material which is already on the 65 ter list or the Prosecution would need to make an application. So I -- I've sought clarification. Mr. Re has given clarification to me this morning that the only documents that the Prosecution seeks to tender through the chain of custody evidence are either documents that have already been marked for identification or tendered, as set out in the first column of the schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, they are not tendered, because most of them are already exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So they're in evidence, but we now receive additional information as to --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: As to where they came from, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- where they came from, and that certainly answers questions in relation to P130 and P234. To that extent, it's good to receive that information. Then we have three documents still to be tendered which are on the 65 ter list, and then there are three remaining documents which are not on the 65 ter list, but where we have to --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Consider, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to consider whether they are actually the same or almost the same documents as we find on the 65 ter list. If they are, it might be easy -- more easy to allow them to be added.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes. May I say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- on the clear understanding that Mr. Re's 99 per cent is, in fact, the correct position, we would have no objection to the six documents that appear on page 3 forming part of the material before the Trial Chamber. So that is both those which are on the 65 ter list but not yet tendered formally through any witness or -- and the three documents that it is sought to adduce that have not been included within the 65 ter list. Having said that, the question then arises as to what is the most efficient way of adducing that evidence of chain of custody, whether it is most efficiently done by calling this witness, who deals with the possession of a briefcase between, as Your Honour postulates, Novi Sad and Belgrade and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- then leaves it in his house and then it goes back to the office, but doesn't deal with the seizure of the documents. Then call another witness later on to talk about the seizure to have documents, who can't deal with what happens between their seizure and their handing over to this witness, and then put that together with a series of -- of declarations dealing with what happens within the OTP. I mean, I'm in the Trial Chamber's hands, but it does seem to be, with respect, that that's a rather cumbersome way of dealing with it. The simplest way of dealing with it would be for the parties to take time out of court to produce a stipulation which goes through for the documents that are set out in the schedule that appears on pages 88 to 91, a stipulation as to chain of custody, so that -- that we don't need to take time with either this witness or, indeed, calling another witness who deals with another part but not the whole of the chain of custody sometime later in the week or next week. Now, obviously, if it's thought preferable to hear witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, for these witnesses, they have given statements, of course, for the witness who's now waiting, Mr. Ralic is waiting to testify, I've some hesitation to send him now back and say the parties start now negotiating on certain matters which --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- might be easily resolved. But I can imagine that talking about the witness who's waiting now that we get his evidence admitted under Rule -- I don't know whether there's any problem with the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There -- there would be a problem with the statement in its current form, so we would need to deal with it. It's not been served on the -- on the Defence either under 92 bis or 92 ter, and so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. At the same time, could that be resolved by redacting the statement? Is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- a huge portion or is it a smaller portion?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: May I say that one of the reasons why I've been trying to deal with this in the way that I have is because I'm conscious of the fact that the simplest way of dealing with this is to take what he has to say and what the others have to say and then produce a simple stipulation that takes the material through. We aren't raising history about this matter. We had notified the Prosecution last week that subject to the clarification of exhibits to be introduced, it wouldn't be necessary for -- we thought it would be unlikely for these witnesses to travel and suggested that their travel arrangements might be put off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And I'm simply concerned that we find ourselves in a position where a motion comes through overnight which for the first time clarifies what the material is, which is the first and the most important question, and then we're in court the next morning with the witness here without the opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- to resolve issues concerning the 92 ter statement. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, of course, the Chamber is concerned about sending the parties out and take the whole of the morning to negotiate, and then to hear as a result that no agreement was reached. I mean, then we would prefer to hear the evidence, rather than ... But what we could do, first of all, Mr. Re, I'd like to hear what your response would be to the suggestion made by Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm in the Trial Chamber's hands here, as I entirely appreciate and take the Trial Chamber's point, Your Honour's point, that the witness is here. I can't see any -- any dispute in his statement, his 92 ter -- what would be a 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, there seems to be a problem. I mean, that's what Mr. Emmerson tells me, and that's what, if we ask the witness in, what we'll find, because I take it that Mr. Emmerson is not telling us that there is a problem if there's no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No. I mean, there's no mystery to it. He -- he deals with what, in fact, happened so far as the suitcase was concerned and his involvement with it, but he also purports to describe the contents of material which is not adduced by the Prosecution by describing a process of analysis within the RDB of the material that was there. And, so, since we've now got clarity as to what it is the Prosecution is proposing to rely upon, I don't want to have a situation where there is evidence in through the 92 ter statement, if that's what it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- which goes beyond that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, in the statement we find some description, which, of course, I have not tried to match with the documents we have now in this annex, so I couldn't say anything about it. It's -- I would say it's mainly for the Defence to -- to find out whether any of, especially the six documents, would fall within the description, would fall outside the description, whether we should admit this as -- as a general description, or whether we should focus on the documents we find on the list now. You say you're in the hands of the Chamber. That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just before the Trial Chamber responds, as I'm sitting here, it occurs to me one practical solution would be to take an early break, and at that stage for the Defence to identify with the Prosecution which paragraphs of the witness statement would need to be redacted, and then see if it could be admitted in that way, if that is the most convenient way of using the witness's presence here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I had a similar thing in mind. I just discussed with Judge Hoepfel that the -- perhaps the most practical way of dealing with it is to give you 40 minutes, 45 minutes, one hour, a limited time, to see whether there's a basis for an agreement. If yes, we'd give you more time to put that agreement on paper; if no, we'd start hearing the witness, who is now waiting. I think one of the things we should do at this moment is to inform the witness about his present situation. But before we do so, we have a few other matters as well. So, therefore, the parties will have an opportunity at an early break to -- to establish whether there's a basis for agreement, yes or no, and then to report to the Chamber within that limited time. We'll then, if the answer is positive, we'll then most likely give you more time to work that out. If the answer is negative, we'll start hearing the evidence to be given by the witness who's waiting at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just a slight correction to something I said earlier on this topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I said there were two documents in the Zyrapi, which you asked for clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are actually three: P130, 225, and 234.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but they're all on the list. Yes, okay. That's, of course. I think the problem would not be the ones who are on the list. Okay. Leave it to that for a moment. There are two other matters. The first is, at least I understood, Mr. Emmerson, that you'd like to be better informed about the further scheduling of this week as far as witnesses are concerned. Is that correct? That's what I understood, or let me just -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It is a concern of the Chamber, let's put it this way --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- so that we all know how we will proceed this week.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a witness for today, and we now know that he might or might not testify. We'll explain the situation to him in a minute. Then we turn into private session, because I do not know exactly which witnesses might still require protective measures.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Being now in open session again, I would like to explain why we were in private session. That is because we discussed scheduling of witnesses where it's still uncertain whether any of these witnesses would -- whether the party calling those witnesses would apply for protective measures; and out of an abundance of caution, we dealt with the matter in private session. Now, as far as videolinks are concerned, because we have more than one videolink pending, to say the least, we'll deal with that after the break. But before we have a break, I would first like to deliver two decisions, and I'd like the witness to be called into the courtroom so that we can briefly explain the present situation. The first decision is on the Prosecution's motion on the proposed witness Fred Abrahams. This is a decision on the Prosecution's motion of November the 5th, 2007 to hear the testimony of Fred Abrahams by videolink on the 12th of November, or, alternatively, to hear the witness face-to-face in The Hague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- yes. I received French translation on the English Channel, but the French translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the French translation now follows us. The last words I spoke were: "Or, alternatively, to hear the witness face-to-face, in The Hague, on the 19th of November; that is, two court days after the scheduled close of the Prosecution's case."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yesterday, the Prosecution informed us that Abrahams would, in fact, not be available for testimony in The Hague until the 20th of November, three days after the scheduled close of the case, and the very date we have set aside for any Rule 98 bis submissions. The two options with which the Prosecution presents the Chamber require a showing of good cause. This is because the usual grounds for granting videolink testimony have not been demonstrated in the case of Abrahams. Good cause also needs to be shown if the Chamber is to extend the Prosecution's case three days, three court days, beyond the scheduled closing date. In neither respects has the Prosecution sought in its motion to demonstrate good cause. In the Chamber's view, good cause might have been shown had the Prosecution demonstrated that Abrahams is an exceptionally important witness for the Prosecution, who could not have been scheduled at an earlier stage of the case. With this in mind, the Chamber has considered the content of Abrahams' proposed Rule 92 ter statement, which is attached to the Prosecution's motion. The Chamber has found that Abrahams' proposed evidence has little or no probative value or is inadmissible on the grounds of prejudice. This means that Abrahams does not fall into the category of an exceptionally important witness for the Prosecution. In explaining this conclusion, the Chamber does not find it necessary to go through every paragraph of Abrahams' statement but will refer only to a subset of paragraphs, which illustrate the problems we have alluded to. Paragraphs 1 through 23 of the statement are background information and add nothing to the case. Paragraphs 24, 50, 53, 58, 63, 65, and 67 through 69 of the statement contain the witness's conclusions on legal matters and on general factual matters of legal significance, which the Chamber itself is tasked to decide in this case. Such opinions are not appropriate evidence from a purported fact witness. The Prosecution's task is to select fact witnesses who, as a rule, are able to relate to the Chamber their own direct experiences of the acts and circumstances alleged in the indictment, in order to enable the Chamber to draw its own conclusions. Abrahams is not such a witness. The Chamber has discouraged the use of so-called summarising witnesses and has urged the Prosecution to minimise reliance on opinion evidence. Many other paragraphs in the proposed Rule 92 ter statement - and thus, many other types of evidence that we are likely to hear from Abrahams, if he were to be called viva voce - are irrelevant, or often completely unsourced, or the opinions of a historian or political scientist, which Abrahams is not, or personal speculations of an entirely unusable variety, or factual claims for which the Chamber has received better evidence from other witnesses and from documents. No disrespect at all is meant to the witness, who is clearly a qualified and successful human rights researcher; rather, the fault lies with the Prosecution for attempting to schedule such a witness at this late stage in the case. The Prosecution has, therefore, not shown good cause for the relief it requests. For that reason, we have decided to deny the motion. This concludes the Chamber's decision. Then I'd like to deliver the following decision on the Prosecution's motion to make testimony of Witness 56 public with redactions. On the 18th of July, 2007, Witness 56 testified before the Chamber by means of videolink. Witness 56 gave his testimony in private session. On the 31st of August, 2007, the Prosecution requested the Chamber to order that the testimony of Witness 56 be made public within -- with certain proposed redactions. On the 10th of September, 2007, the Balaj Defence asked the Chamber to deny the request, arguing that the question of the admissibility of Witness 56's testimony should be resolved first, and only then status of Witness 56's testimony. The Balaj Defence also submitted that it is doubtful whether Witness 56's testimony could be sufficiently redacted to prevent disclosure of his identity. Given the nature of Witness 56's testimony, the Chamber agrees with the Balaj Defence that Witness 56's testimony cannot be sufficiently redacted to prevent the disclosure of his identity; therefore, the Prosecution's request is denied. The Chamber will allow the parties five minutes to make oral submissions on the admissibility of Witness 56's evidence on Thursday, the 8th of November, 2007, should they wish to do so. In case the parties expect to need more than five minutes, they are invited to file written submissions with a maximum of five pages by the 12th of November, 2007, 5.00 p.m. This concludes the Chamber's decision. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. If I might, with regard to that issue. We need to edit the written submission that we have in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have, of course, received already submissions on your part.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it seemed --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of the admissibility, since we haven't heard anything, we have a motion in preparation, but we're going to need to do some editing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, in your earlier submission, you said that the parties should be invited to make further submissions. If you have carefully listened, there was no invitation at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But there was an opportunity given to the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, you, the parties, are always free to file motions. If you have to redact a motion you've already prepared, then we'll see its final version.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We were just about ready to send it off, but we'll hold back now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I would like to explain to the witness the present situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ralic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ralic, it must be unpleasant if -- can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It must be unpleasant to be in a small room waiting for well over an hour if you expect to be called at 9.00 to testify. It might even be more unpleasant if you are then escorted into a courtroom and once over the doorstep are taken out again. The Chamber apologises for this. Mr. Ralic, I'd like to explain the present situation. You are called by the Prosecution as a witness, and the Chamber has read your statement you earlier gave. Your testimony would be about the chain of custody of documents, when you received them, where you took them. Okay. Now, you may understand that to get the complete picture, we'd need to hear more evidence, perhaps from persons who know more about it, or persons who might have been present when they were seized, or at least have more information about other parts of the trajectory of these documents. Now, the parties have suggested to the Chamber that there may be a possibility to prevent all of these witnesses to come to The Hague and to testify, but the parties need a bit more time to further discuss whether they could agree on these matters. Until this morning, it was also not entirely clear what documents would be covered by such testimony, and the parties appear to be ready to further elaborate an agreement on that. Under those circumstances, the Chamber as granted the parties the next hour to further discuss whether we can avoid people traveling to The Hague if there is another possibility which would be more economic both in terms of time and money. Mr. Ralic, you are more or less a victim of this situation because you were the first one. You travelled already to The Hague; nevertheless, the Chamber would ask you perhaps to be patient for the next hour. If the parties are unable to reach such a level of agreement that the Chamber could be confident that a final agreement can be reached, we would hear your testimony. If, however, the parties would report to the Chamber within approximately one hour from now that there is a solid basis for an agreement, then there would be no need to hear your testimony any more. That is not to say that your information under those circumstances would have been useless. I would say not at all, because certainly that information will be included in the communication between the parties trying to find an agreement on the matters dealt with in your statement. So I would like you to ask to be even more patient for the next hour, and you know that depends on what the parties can achieve, whether there's any need to hear your evidence. If there's no need to hear your evidence, then, of course, it is a pity that you spent your precious time on traveling to The Hague and, of course, also psychologically preparing for your testimony. But under those circumstances, the Chamber, unfortunately, will have to decide that the more economic way, both in terms of time and money, would be the appropriate one and would, under those circumstances, beg for your understanding for such a decision. So, therefore, we ask for more patience on your side. You may now follow the usher, who will escort you. I hope at least you get sufficient coffee, so that you are treated well. Would you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I turn into private session for one more second.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. I'd just seek a clarification in relation to the -- the ruling you made a few moments ago in relation to Witness 56 and the five minutes that the parties -- for the parties each to address the Trial Chamber in relation to what you described as the admissibility of his evidence. I'd just seek a clarification so we can prepare ourselves for our five minutes if we wish to avail ourselves; namely, by "admissibility," does the Trial Chamber mean the weight, if any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- if any, to be given to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. From what I remember, but correct me if I'm wrong, there was an issue of making the solemn declaration. The witness, finally, did not manage to pronounce the words; although, I tried to make him pronounce these words. Now, he said a lot of other things. What the consequences would be for the admissibility of the evidence after this start, I think that's the first issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then, of course, if the parties would say anything about consistency or inconsistency, that is a matter for which I would say the parties could argue that it would be an admissibility or a weight issue. It goes without saying that if you consider it to be a weight issue, then, of course, the Chamber will, as always, of course, carefully look at the evidence and to see to what extent it is reliable, credible, and consistent. But I also can imagine that a party would argue that under certain circumstances issues which are usually within the realm of reliability, credibility, and consistency, could reach a level at which admissibility would become an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The only query I have is the evidence is on the trial record. It's a -- is it a position of whether you disregard the evidence or whether you would then be satisfied that the evidence is there; we will give it some weight --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- disregard it, because it's already on the trial record. That's my concern as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the trial record. But, of course, the parties could argue -- if a witness would appear here and if I would ask him to give his name and he would give his date of birth, if I would then ask him whether he was born at a certain place and he would answer that he was born on the North Pole and give no proper explanation for that, then we might reach a moment where we say although his answers to the questions are on the record, whether you call that to disregard that or whether you call that that it could not be admitted, because it's not really -- it's words pronounced by a person who apparently cannot serve as a witness, then, of course, I must say that we'd have to think then about whether it's an admissibility issue. It could well be. Although, if witnesses are answering to questions not always in the way we expect them to answer questions, then sometimes to be not fully consistent in every respect, then, of course, that would not immediately to -- lead to conclusions as to the admissibility of that testimony but would, rather, go to weight. So where exactly to draw that line is an issue, I can imagine, the parties would like to address in their five minutes or in their written submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think the issue of -- that you focused on the issues that do exist with regard that this witness's situation and whether or not, for purposes of an admissibility to conversation, a discussion -- an exclusion from the trial record or whether or not it's appropriately part of a trial record is something we can -- we can grapple with in our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is rather a technical matter, then; and, of course, the Chamber is mainly interested in the substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We're focused mainly on the substance, but since the technical matter was raised, I wanted to respond to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Chamber is looking forward to your oral or written submissions. I now suggest that we take a break for -- until 11.30. Would that give sufficient time to ...? Yes. Then we'll adjourn until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked myself what would be the best way to proceed. I'll do the following: The Chamber was briefed by one of their legal officers on what the legal officer understood the present situation was. I'll try to give that; and if there's then anything to be added, then -- or if there's anything incorrect in that, the Chamber would like to hear from the parties. The Chamber was informed by -- through the legal officer that the parties had reached an agreement on the chain of custody evidence to be presented, and that there would be no need to hear testimony in court on this matter. That's the first issue. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That is correctly understood. But may I, for the avoidance of any doubt, hand up to the Chamber copies of the product of the work that's taken place. Perhaps if the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is a joint ... Mr. Usher, could you ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll have a look at it. I see that I receive copies - I'll give one to the registrar - that is a one A4 piece of paper, on top "Chain of custody," containing ten items. Mr. Re, that's also the document you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It is. It's the agreement in principle. I don't think Mr. Emmerson is asking it to be received onto the record. We will put it into a nicer form with a heading on it and attach the annex to it, but that's the -- and there's a couple of spelling errors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But that's the agreement in principle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So this is the agreement. Now, I want a commitment of the parties that the Chamber will keep this. It is not evidence. The Chamber will wait for further submissions. If a new battle starts on these submissions, the Chamber requires the parties to commit themselves to any decision then to be taken by the Chamber, if there's still new --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- elements arise out of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I just make two observations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: First of all, I don't think either of us anticipates any change in this position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Secondly, so that it's absolutely clear for purposes of record, what items 1 to 10 are -- is a summary of the evidence that Prosecution would elicit. The Defence for very obvious reasons is not in a position to confirm the accuracy of the content of that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- information, but neither is the Defence in a position to dispute it. So it is on that basis; in other words, there is a summary of the evidence that would otherwise have to be adduced or heard by the Trial Chamber that the stipulation would be made, on the basis, as I said, that the Defence is not in a position to dispute it. So with that -- with that explanation, we do not anticipate on either side any significant changes to the document as it appears, other than typographical errors and other matters of a very formal character.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, as far as the documents covered, we find them in an Annex A, which is not here yet, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It isn't there yet. But if Your Honour looks at the footnote, Annex A is the list of 20 documents identified at pages 88 to 91 of the motion filed yesterday, and that annex is headed in the motion "Documents on the Prosecution's Rule 65 ter list originating from the 24 binders received from BIA in November 2005," and that relates to item 9. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then -- I'm trying to read through it very quickly. Does this mean -- earlier this morning, we discussed a list which contained three subsets; one being 65 ter -- already MFI'd or exhibited; then three appearing on the 65 ter list, although not yet admitted. So I understand these to be included in Annex A. Then the third portion was three documents which were similar too. I do not find them here. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: No, they are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: They are there. They are included within the 20 documents referred to; therefore, the Defence waives any objection to the addition to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. So the whole of that list we discussed this morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So each of the document is contained within the schedule that we drew attention to this morning at the relevant pages of the motion, and that is what will be Annex A.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, for purposes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, for purposes of clarification on that very specific point, there are 20 documents. Fourteen of those documents obtain the first position that already having -- already have been admitted. Three are on the 65 ter list; three are not, so it's 14 plus 3 plus 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We get that list. There are 20 documents on that list. So if any -- the parties will now work on giving it a different format, but basically saying this. If the parties then, on minor matters, would start quarreling again - which I do not expect, as a matter of fact - then I do understand that there is a commitment of both parties, and that would include all three Defence counsel. Isn't it, Mr. Guy-Smith and Mr. Troop? I see Mr. Troop nodding "yes." Mr. Guy-Smith already adhered to it. Then the Chamber will establish what the agreement is, after having heard the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just for the Chamber's peace of mind, there's been no quarreling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: This has been resolved by, if I may say so, cooperation, reducing the need for the calling of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: So far as -- well, Your Honour is going to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson, is there anything to be added?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Not in respect of that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Re, anything you would like to add on this matter? No. Okay. Then I'll continue for the next one. I'll tell you what information the Chamber received, and then we'll see whether that's correct or not, but we have to go into private session for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Being in open session again, in private session the Chamber gave a decision in which it grants the request by the Prosecutor to hear the testimony of Witness 23 through videolink. The reasons will follow. The final thing I'd like to do is to explain to the witness, who has been waiting all morning, that unfortunate for him but, of course, fortunate for the Chamber, that we don't have to examine him, that he doesn't have to testify. Mr. Re, is there anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's fine. Just while the usher is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: To use the time, there are several outstanding summaries. Could we possibly take the time to read those onto the record? I think it might take about ten, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have no witness for tomorrow, do we?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Chamber would prefer to use the time tomorrow for those matters and not today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I only say that because it's pretty boring listening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, boring or not, we have to organise our work also in such a way that we can stay ahead of all quick developments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ralic, I earlier informed you today about ongoing discussions between the parties to seek an agreement on the chain of custody of documents the parties want -- have to some extent already tendered and that were already admitted into evidence. Unfortunately for you, the parties did reach an agreement. That's, of course, very fortunate for the Chamber, because it saves time and it saves money as well. I said "unfortunately for you" because you have spent your time already on traveling to The Hague. Therefore, I think I would speak on behalf of the parties that if they could have avoided the present situation, where you could have refrained from traveling to The Hague, they certainly would have wished to achieve this result at an earlier stage without bothering you to travel to The Hague. Nevertheless, it would be useless to hear your evidence, but I can assure you that the information which was found in your statement has been used in reaching an agreement. I saw references to your statement, so don't get the impression that what you earlier told the Office of the Prosecution in your statement is -- has not turned out to be useful. Nevertheless, no testimony in court. I thank you, I would say, more than average for coming to The Hague, where you didn't have to testify, and I hope that you'll be back home soon and that you have a safe trip home again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any other matter to be raised at this moment? No other matters to be raised. We will adjourn until tomorrow, Thursday, the 8th of November, quarter past 2.00 [sic], Courtroom II -- III. Yes, I'm ignoring the signals by Mr. Registrar. Thank you for correcting me, Mr. Registrar. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of November, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 12.35 p.m.,
